INTEREST OF AMICI CURIAE
The Second Amendment Institute (“SAI”) is a
nonprofit educational organization dedicated to
educating, activating, and empowering Americans to
defend the right to keep and bear arms. Founded in
2016, SAI conducts public education, publishes
commentary, and supports litigation concerning the
Second Amendment. Its members and supporters
include citizens who possess or wish to possess
semiautomatic rifles for defense of self, family,
community, and country. SAI therefore has a direct
interest in ensuring that the Court does not permit
lower courts to sever the Amendment’s operative
guarantee from its declared object—the security of a
free state—or to transform a rifle’s suitability for
common defense into a reason to exclude it from
constitutional protection.
Individual amici Yzaguirre and Ayala are
members of SAI and possess semiautomatic rifles
such as are at issue in this case and would acquire
additional such rifles if legal to do so.1
SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT
The Second Amendment’s guarantee of an
individual right to arms is  settled, but its underlying
purpose been neglected by the lower courts’ mistaken
laser focus on individual self-defense. District of
Columbia v. Heller, 554 U.S. 570 (2008) held the

1 No counsel for a party authored this brief in whole or in part,
and no person other than amici, its members, or its counsel made
a monetary contribution intended  to fund the preparation or
submission of this brief. See Sup. Ct. R. 37.6.

2


operative clause secures an individual right to arms
unconnected to actual militia service. Id. at 595, 598–
600 (2008). Yet Heller also insisted that “logic
demands” a connection between the prefatory clause
and the right it announces. Id. at 577. The
Amendment undoubtedly protects individual selfdefense, but its protection of an individual right to
arms is grounded on the preservation of a citizen
militia. The amendment’s two clauses are not
enemies. The individual right to arms is the
constitutional means; the security of a free state is the
announced end.
That end matters here. The founding generation
feared a government possessing a standing army
could disable popular resist ance by disarming the
body of the people. The constitutional answer was not
a government-issued right to  report for duty. It was
the preservation of the pre-existing right of citizens to
keep and bear their own arms—ready for personal
defense, militia service, resistance to domestic
tyranny, and defense against foreign invasion. See
Heller, 554 U.S. at 597-98; Clinton Rossiter ed., The
Federalist Papers, 299–300 (No. 46, James Madison)
(1961). These purposes drive the determination of
what arms are protected.
United States v. Miller, 307 U.S. 174 (1939) applied
exactly that understanding. It asked whether a shortbarreled shotgun had a “reasonable relationship to the
preservation or efficiency of a well regulated militia.”
Id. at 178. The Court did not exclude military arms as
would the 7 th Circuit. See Bevis v. City of Naperville,
85 F.4th 1175, 1182, 1194-95 (7 th Cir. 2023). Rather,

3


Miller treated militia suitability as the reason an arm
would be protected, while finding the record
insufficient as to a short-barreled shotgun. 307 U.S at
178–83. Heller translated Miller’s holding into
modern terms: protected arms are those “in common
use at the time,” because citizens historically
appeared for militia duty bearing lawful arms they
kept at home. 554 U.S. at 624–25, 627. See also
Caetano v. Massachusetts . 577 U.S. 411, 416 (2016)
(Alito, J., concurring).
The decisions below invert that rule. The Seventh
Circuit in Viramontes v. County of Cook, Viramontes,
2025 U.S. App. LEXIS 13331 (7 th Cir. June 2, 2025),
followed its decision in Bevis, which divined a
supposed divide between “civilian” arms and arms of
military capability. 85 F.4th at 1192–94.  Nat'l Ass'n
for Gun Rights  v. Lamont , 153 F.4th 213 (2d Cir.
2025), cert. granted  sub nom. Grant v. Higgins, 2026
WL 1871312 (U.S. June 30, 2026) (hereinafter
“Grant”), likewise treated the AR-15’s effectiveness,
military lineage, and alleged reduced utility for closequarters self-defense as reasons it falls outside of the
right. See Id. at 241–42. But the Constitution does not
protect a rifle only to the extent it does not resemble a
military arm. The textual inquiry asks whether the
object is a bearable arm. New York State Rifle and
Pistol Association v. Bruen, 597 U.S. 1, 28 (2022). If it
is, it is presumptively protected and the government
must justify its ban by historical tradition. Id. at 24,
33–34. With respect to the rifles at issue here, that is
a tall order because the AR -15 platform rifle is the
very type of commonly possessed arm a citizen would
possess for militia service even beyond the

4


overwhelming evidence it is widely possessed for
individual self-defense.
Although Heller focused on handguns for
individual self-defense, as that was the issue in that
case, the Court acknowledged the amendment’s
purpose to ensure an arme d citizenry able to provide
for the common defense. See 554 U.S. at 602-03
(discussing state constitutional provisions, inter alia,
protecting the right for common defense). See also
Robert Leider, The Individual Right to Bear Arms for
Common Defense 1–5, 27–43, SSRN No. 4918009
(2024) (hereinafter “Leide r”). As Professor Leider
explains, the Constitution contemplates dual land
forces: a professional standing army and an amateur
militia drawn from the people. Id. at 16–29. The
Second Amendment preserve s citizens’ capacity to
serve as amateur soldiers, prevents professional or
select armed factions from monopolizing the tools of
force, reduces dependence on a permanent military
establishment, and maintains a final check against
usurpation. See Id.  at 27–30. That theory gives
operative force to every word of the Amendment and
explains why rifles suitable for common defense—not
merely weapons used for private quarrels—stand at
its center.
Because the decisions below prohibit possession of
commonly owned rifles on the basis of alleged military
features the decisions below conflict with the very
purpose for which the Second Amendment was
ratified. As such the decisions below must be reversed.

5


ARGUMENT
I. The Militia Purpose Confirms—Rather Than
Narrows—The Individual Right To Keep
Rifles Capable Of Common Defense.
A. Heller preserved the logical connection
between the Amendment’s two clauses.
The Second Amendment begins with a proposition
of political theory: “A well regulated Militia” is
“necessary to the security of a free State.” U.S. Const.
amend. II. It then states a legal rule to preserve that
institution: “the right of the people to keep and bear
Arms, shall not be infringed.” Id. Heller correctly
rejected the claim that the first clause confines the
right to persons acting under government command.
554 U.S. at 577–600. “The people,” as in the First and
Fourth Amendments, means members of the political
community who hold individual rights. Id. at 579–81.
“Keep” meant possess, and “bear” meant carry for
confrontation. Id. at 581–92.
But Heller did not erase the preface. A prefatory
clause may resolve ambiguity but must remain
logically connected to the operative command . Id. at
577–78. Heller thus returned to the militia clause to
confirm its reading. The militia was not a small statecreated corps. It comprised the body of citizens
capable of acting together for common defense . Id. at
595–96. Those citizens or dinarily supplied arms
themselves. Id. at 624, citing Miller, 307 U.S. at 179.
The Federalists’ assurance was that an armed
population, organized when necessary by the states,
would check both invasion and a potentially

6


oppressive standing army. See The Federalist Papers
at 184 (No. 29, Alexander Hamilton); Id.  at 299–300
(No. 46, James Madison).
The 1792 Militia Act made the architecture
concrete. Every enrolled able-bodied white male
citizen was required to “provide himself” with a
musket or firelock, bayonet, ammunition, and related
equipment. Act of May 8, 1792, ch. 33, § 1, 1 Stat. 271.
The arm was privately ac quired and kept, then
brought when called to service. The institution
depended on antecedent civilian possession of militia
suitable arms. Illinois and Connecticut cannot
preserve that design while forbidding possession of an
ordinary rifle particularly suited for militia service.
This understanding does not reduce the right to
one of collective service. It explains why the right was
an individual right. A militia that may exist only after
the government chooses to arm it cannot check the
government’s decision to disarm it. As Heller put it,
the founding-era fear was that the Federal
Government would disarm the people in order to
disable this citizens’ militia, enabling a politicized
standing army or a select militia to rule. See 554 U.S.
at 598-99. The remedy was to deny government the
power to abridge the people ’s pre-existing right. Id.;
see McDonald v. City of Chicago, 561 U.S. 742, 770–78
(2010) (plurality opinion)  (recounting the right’s
importance against public and private violence).
At the founding, militia functions included
repelling invasion, suppressing insurrection,
enforcing law, and responding when regular forces
were absent. U.S. Const. art.  I, § 8, cls. 15. The same

7


citizen may keep one arm for household defense today
and common defense tomorrow. The Constitution does
not divide the object according to the owner’s
momentary purpose.
B. The Amendment preserves an individual
right for common defense.
Modern Second Amendment doctrine has often
presented a false choice. One theory says the
Amendment protects a collective entitlement of states
or organized militia units; another says it protects an
individual’s choice of a firearm solely for defense
against ordinary crime. Profes sor Leider identifies a
historically grounded third position: the right belongs
to individuals, but its expressly announced public
purpose is common defense. See Leider, supra, at 1–
16. The holder of the right is the citizen. The protected
conduct includes acquiring, keeping, carrying, and
training with suitable arms. The constitutional
beneficiary is both the individual and the political
community whose security depends on a population
capable of military service. See Id. at 5–16, 36–40.
That synthesis answers the standard objection
that citizens outside an organized unit cannot invoke
a militia-related right. Th e founding militia had two
related meanings: the body of citizens capable of
bearing arms and the portion actually enrolled or
called into service. See Heller , 554 U.S. at 595–96;
Leider, supra, at 29 n. 203. Congress may decide
whom to organize, when to train them, and how to
discipline them. U.S. Const. art. I, § 8, cl. 16. But the
antecedent capacity of the people to furnish
themselves with arms cannot depend on Congress

8


first choosing to organize them. If governmental
inaction could extinguish the right, the political
branches could accomplish by neglect the
disarmament the Amendment forbids directly.
The distinction between ri ght and duty is equally
important. The Second Amendment secures liberty to
acquire and train with arms; it does not itself
conscript every right-hold er. Madison’s proposed
conscientious-objector la nguage—providing that a
person religiously scrupulous of bearing arms should
not be compelled to render military service—
underscores that a right he ld broadly could coexist
with narrower legal duties of service. See 1 Annals of
Cong. 451 (1789) (Joseph Gales, ed.1834); Leider,
supra, at 30. The right therefore belongs to “the
people,” including those not presently enrolled,
because preserving broad civilian capacity is the
necessary foundation for any future call to common
defense.
C. Common defense includes defense against
invasion, insurrection, and usurpation.
Justice Story described the militia as the “natural
defence of a free country” against three dangers:
“sudden foreign invasions,” “domestic insurrections,”
and “domestic usurpations of power by rulers.” 3
Joseph Story, Commentaries on the Constitution §
1890, at 746 (1833). Each danger explains why
privately kept military -suitable arms matter.
Invasion may require rapid mobilization before
regular forces can arrive. Insurrection may overwhelm
ordinary civil officers. Usurpation presents the harder
constitutional case because the threat may come from

9


those who command public force. A population capable
of common defense supplie s resilience against all
three.
This anti-usurpation function is not a license for
private violence or a judicially administered right to
revolt whenever a citizen dislikes public policy.
Government retains authority to punish assault,
rebellion, intimidation, and misuse of arms. See U.S.
Const. art. I, § 8, cl. 15; 18 U.S.C. §§ 2383–2384. The
structural point is different: the Constitution
deliberately denied government a complete monopoly
over ordinary arms. An ar med population raises the
cost of unlawful seizure of power, makes exclusive
reliance on professional soldiers less necessary, and
helps keep coercive power aligned with the citizenry.
See Leider, supra, at 27-28. Constitutional structure
often operates prospectively by preventing dangerous
concentrations of power; it need not wait for the feared
abuse to occur.
The precise equipment and organization of modern
forces have changed, but Caetano forbids freezing
constitutional protection to eighteenth-century
technology. See 577 U.S. at 411–12. The enduring
principle is civilian capacity. A modern semiautomatic
rifle commonly possessed and suitable for individual
defensive use is closer to  the privately supplied
musket or rifle of the founding scheme than is a
weapon selected precisely because it lacks utility
beyond a private altercation.

10


D. The concern with standing armies was
with professionalized coercive power.
The framing-era objection was not that a national
standing army might interfere with state military
prerogatives. It was that a permanent, professional
force could become a separate armed faction with
interests, discipline, and political leverage distinct
from the people. See Leider, supra, at 20–23. A
standing army was more proficient than a citizen
militia, but that proficien cy carried constitutional
risks: separation from civilian society, expense and
taxation, executive use of soldiers for domestic
enforcement, and the possibility that rulers could
employ a concentrated armed body against the public.
Id.
The Second Amendment’s compromise did not
forbid a standing army or transfer military
sovereignty to the states. Congress retained power to
raise armies, organize the militia, prescribe uniform
arms, and create select units. U.S. Const. art. I, § 8,
cls. 12–16. What the Amendment did was preserve the
foundation of the universal militia system: the
political community’s ability to acquire, keep, and
become proficient with arms. Leider, supra, at 26–28.
Congress could regulate the militia—put it in good
order—but regulation could not become destruction.
That structural compromise serves three related
ends. First, professional and select armed bodies
cannot enjoy a legal monopoly on the tools of violence.
Second, a pool of armed civilians reduces the degree to
which the Nation must depend on full-time soldiers in
peacetime. Third, the distribution of military capacity

11


supplies a check against abuse of power. Leider,
supra, at 27–28. A doctrine that protects handguns
but permits government to prohibit the ordinary rifle
most readily adapted to common defense preserves
the individual personal protective aspects of the
Second Amendment while weakening all three of the
structural ends discussed above.
E. Nineteenth century cases placed militarysuitable arms at the right’s core.
Nineteenth century cases do not support a civilianversus-military dichotomy. To the contrary, even
courts adopting a compar atively narrow view of the
right to keep and bear arms treated militia-type
weapons as protected.
Aymette v. State,  21 Tenn. (2 Hum.) 154 (1840).
construed Tennessee’s guarantee that citizens may
bear arms “for their common defence.” Its description
of protected arms is powerf ul evidence that weapons
of military utility are protected. Aymette said the
constitutional term “arms” referred to weapons
“usually employed in civili zed warfare” and that the
citizen had an unqualified right to keep a weapon “of
the character before described.” Id. at 158, 160. Rifles,
muskets, swords, and similar arms of the citizensoldier were not excluded as “weapons of war;”
military usefulness in fact defined the protected
category. Id. at 158–61.
Nunn v. State, 1 Ga. 243, 251 (1846). reached the
right’s individual dimension and invalidated a
prohibition on openly carrying pistols and other arms.
It described the object of the Second Amendment as

12


preserving the “right of the whole people” to keep and
bear arms so that a well-regulated militia could be
reared and qualified. Id. That formulation joins
individual possession to collective security without
collapsing one into the other.
Presser v. Illinois,  116 U.S. 252, 264–66 (1886)
likewise distinguished a state’s authority to prohibit
unauthorized private military companies from any
authority to disarm the people. Presser held that
states could regulate bodies of men drilling as military
organizations, id. at 267–68 but emphasized they
could not “prohibit the p eople from keeping and
bearing arms” so as to deprive the United States of its
reserve military force, id. at 265. Incorporation
doctrine has since change d the decision’s federalism
framework. See McDonald , 561 U.S. at 750, 791.
Nonetheless, Presser’s recognition that the body of
armed citizens remained available for public defense
nevertheless confirms the historic relationship
between private keeping and military readiness.
Miller synthesized this tradition. The Court found
no evidence in the record that a short-barreled
shotgun bore a reasonable relationship to militia
efficiency, and therefore could not judicially notice
that the Second Amendment protected it. 307 U.S. at
178. The premise was that militia-suitable arms
receive protection. Miller explained that the militia
comprised civilians “physically capable of acting in
concert for the common defense;” when called, they
were “expected to appear bearing arms supplied by
themselves and of the kind in common use at the
time.” Id. at 179. It then surveyed laws requiring

13


citizens to furnish muskets, firelocks, rifles, bayonets,
and ammunition. Id. at 179–82.
Heller did not disturb Miller’s holding. It said
Miller’s basis was that the Second Amendment
protects the kind of weapon that has a “reasonable
relationship to the preservation or efficiency of a well
regulated militia,” 554 U.S. at 622, and it rejected the
dissent’s effort to convert that reasoning into a
limitation requiring the possessor to be enrolled in an
organized service. Id at 622–25. Heller’s “common use”
phrase is therefore not a free-floating popularity
contest. It describes the practical mechanism of a
citizen militia: people br ing the lawful arms they
commonly possess to militia service. Id. at 624–25. See
also Caetano, 577 U.S. at 416 (Alito, J., concurring).
Leading nineteenth-century commentators
agreed. Justice Story called the militia “the natural
defence of a free country” against invasion, domestic
insurrection, and rulers’ usurpation, and warned that
indifference could undermine it. 3 Joseph Story,
Commentaries on the Constitution § 1890, at 746–47.
Thomas Cooley explained that to bear arms “implies
the learning to handle and use them in a way that
makes those who keep them ready for their efficient
use” in the militia and the arms protected “are such as
are suitable for the general defence of the community
against invasion or oppression….” Thomas M. Cooley,
General Principles of Constitutional Law 271 (1880).
Modern scholarship reache s the same conclusion.
Military-suitable arms were unanimously understood
by 19th Century state courts and commentators to be
protected, even amid disagreement over concealable

14


weapons and modes of carry. William Baude & Robert
Leider, The General-Law Right to Bear Arms, 99
Notre Dame L. Rev. 1467, 1500–01 (2024).
Andrews v. State  made the relationship explicit.
The right existed to preserve arms that would
contribute to the efficiency of the citizen as a soldier
and be useful in the common defense. See 50 Tenn. (3
Heisk.) 165, 178–79 (1871). English v. State,  35 Tex.
473, 476 (1872) similarly described protected arms as
“the arms of a militiaman or soldier.” Fife v. State, 31
Ark. 455, 460–61 (1876) treated “the rifle, of all
descriptions, the shot gun, the musket and repeater”
as within the constitution al class while excluding a
small pocket revolver. These courts disagreed about
some weapons and carrying practices, but their
disagreements occurred against shared ground: arms
of the citizen-soldier were pr otected, not disqualified
by military usefulness. See Leider, supra, at 43–45;
Baude & Leider, supra, at 1500–1501.
The common-defense account also explains
Presser’s otherwise puzzling distinction. Illinois could
prohibit an unauthorized private military company
from drilling in public because government may
regulate collective military organizations. 116 U.S. at
267–68. But the state could not disarm the citizenry
and thereby destroy the re serve military resource
upon which public security depended. Id. at 265. The
right protects individual capacity; it does not create
independent private armies. That distinction answers
any objection that recognizing the militia purpose of
the Second Amendment constitutionalizes paramilitary
organizations.

15


II. The Decisions Below Invert Miller, Misread
Heller, And Evade Bruen.
A. Viramontes inherits Bevis’s categorical
military-versus-civilian error.
Cook County prohibits possession, acquisition, and
transfer of numerous semiautomatic rifles, including
AR-15s by name and others by features. Viramontes,
2025 U.S. App. LEXIS 13331, at *2. The Seventh
Circuit affirmed the district court’s dismissal because
it regarded the clai m as foreclosed by Bevis, 85 F.4th
1175, and faulted petitioners for not developing a
record sufficient to di stinguish that ruling. Id. at *3-
5.
Bevis began from a false premise, however. It
appeared to read Heller to say that the sole purpose of
the Second Amendment was to protect armed selfdefense. 85 F.4 th at 1192. And it drew a distinction
between “civilian” weapon s on one side and weapons
“reserved for military use” on the other, then asked
whether prohibited semiautomatic rifles were more
like handguns or machineguns. Id. at 1192–94, 1197.
That distinction meant that
[i]n order to show a likelihood of success
on the merits, the plaintiffs in each of
the cases before us thus have the burden
of showing that the weapons addressed
in the pertinent legislation are Arms
that ordinary people would keep at home
for purposes of self-defense, not weapons
that are exclusively or predominantly
useful in military se rvice, or weapons

16


that are not possessed for lawful
purposes.
Id. at 1194. Because the record did not convince the
court that AR-15-type rifles  materially differed from
military arms, it treated them as potentially outside
the Amendment. Id. at 1195–97. Viramontes carried
that error from an interloc utory record into a final
judgment. 2025 U.S. App. LEXIS 13331, at *4-5.
That is Miller upside down. Miller asked whether
the weapon has militia utility as a reason for coverage.
307 U.S. at 178. Bevis treated military utility as a
reason for exclusion. 85 F.4 th at 1194. The error is
especially stark because the challenged ordinances
identify rifles by features associated with effective
use: adjustable stocks, pistol grips, barrel shrouds,
flash suppressors, and capacity to accept detachable
magazines, etc. See Cook County, Ill., Code §§ 54-211,
54-212 (2024). A governme nt cannot transform the
Second Amendment’s stated purpose into a drafting
guide for prohibitions.
Bevis’s two-pole spectrum—handguns at one end,
machineguns at the other—has no basis in the
constitutional text. See 85 F.4th at 1193. “Arms” does
not mean weapons that judges believe are sufficiently
civilian.2 Heller defined the term broadly as weapons
of offense or armor of defense and held that all

2 Bevis’s logic was that since Heller said machineguns can be
banned, a firearm similar to a machinegun can be banned. See
Id. at 1195.  But that is a misreading of Heller. Bevis failed to
acknowledge that Heller explains that the guns that can be
banned are “arms that are highly unusual in society at large.”
554 U.S. at 627. That is certainly the case with machineguns,
and certainly not the case with AR-15s and similar modern rifles.

17


bearable arms receive prima facie protection. 554 U.S.
at 582. Nor does Miller establish a continuum under
which protection shrinks as a weapon becomes more
capable of common defense. Miller asks whether an
arm has a relevant relationship to a well regulated
militia; it most assuredly does not authorize courts to
deny protection because the relationship is too strong.
See 307 U.S. at 178–83.
Bevis’s record-based framing compounds the error.
The difference between automatic and semiautomatic
fire is a legal and mechanical fact: an ordinary
semiautomatic rifle fires one round per function of the
trigger; an M-16 may fire multiple rounds with one
function of the trigger. Staples v. United States , 511
U.S. 600, 602 & n.1 (1994). Whether a semiautomatic
rifle is a bearable arm does not depend on dueling
experts. And whether millions of citizens may keep
one cannot turn on a court’s impression that
challengers failed to prove enough factual distance
from a rarely possessed weapon the federal
government heavily regulates. Constitutional
coverage is determined by text informed by history,
not a judicial weapons-similarity trial.
Bevis also misplaced the constitutional burden.
Once plaintiffs show they seek to possess bearable
arms, the Second Amendment’s plain text covers the
conduct; the government must then demonstrate the
restriction’s consistency wi th historical tradition.
Bruen, 597 U.S. at 24, 33–34. Bevis instead required
plaintiffs to prove at “step one,” through a fact-heavy
comparison, that their rifles  were sufficiently unlike
the military M-16 machinegun. See 85 F.4th at 1192–

18


97. Viramontes repeated that the plaintiffs bore the
burden to show textual protection “viewed through
the lens of historical tradition.” 2025 U.S. App. LEXIS
13331, at *3-4. That merges Bruen’s two steps and
transfers the government’s historical burden to the
right-holder contrary to this Court’s clear directives.
Wolford v. Lopez, 609 U.S. __, slip op. (June 25,
2026)  clarified the methodology of text first and
history second. See Id. at 7-8. In determining whether
a law clashes with the plain text, three questions
arise: First, does the law apply to “the people”—which
is to say, to “all members of the political community”?
Id. at 7, quoting Heller, 554 U.S. at 580. Second, does
it concern any form of “Ar ms,” i.e., any weapon
customarily used for offensive or defensive purposes?
Id., citing Heller, 554 U.S. at 584.3 Third, does the law
place any restrictions on either the “keep[ing]” (i.e.,
possession) or the “bear[ing]” (i.e., carrying) of arms?
Id., citing Bruen, 597 U.S. at 32-33. Plainly the
answer to each of these questions here is “Yes.”
Justice Barrett’s concurring opinion underscored
the  majority’s discussion of Bruen’s Step One
methodology and eschewed any attempt to import
additional requirements into the Bruen Step One
analysis, for example, supposed historical limitations
on the right.

3  Arms customarily used for offense or defense the Court
elsewhere noted, refers to implements used for offense or
defense, such as handguns that  are “overwhelmingly chosen by
American society” for self-defense. See Heller, 554 U.S. at 628.

19


Addressing the dissent’s proposed use of history to
delimit the meaning of the Second Amendment’s text,
Justice Barrett in her concurring opinion explained:
No one disputes that the Second
Amendment’s text has a fixed meaning
that must be satisfied before a law is
deemed presumptively unconstitutional.
See ante, at 7 (identifying “three
subsidiary questions” that must be
answered at Bruen’s first step). The
disagreement is instead whether courts
can smuggle additional limits, drawn
from our regulatory tradition, into the
plain-text stage of the inquiry. The
answer is and always has been no.
Wolford, concurring slip op. at n.1 (Barrett, J.).
The proper textual threshold then is straightforward. The semiautomatic rifles at issue here are
instruments that can be ca rried and used offensively
or defensively; they are therefore “Arms.” Heller, 554
U.S. at 581–82. Historical limitations enter at the
government’s justification for a restriction at Bruen
Step Two, not by narrowing “Arms” through modern
judicial policy judgments. See Bruen, 597 U.S. at 19,
22–25.
B. Grant converts functional usefulness into
a constitutional defect and substitutes
balancing for history.
The Second Circuit’s decision in Grant rests on the
same inversion. It acknowledged that Connecticut
defines prohibited rifles through “military-style

20


features,” including folding or telescoping stocks,
pistol grips, forward grip s, flash suppressors, and
launcher mounts. Nat’l Ass’n for Gun Rights , 153
F.4th at 225–26. Yet it treated those features, the
AR-15’s military lineage, an d evidence of rapid fire
capability as reasons to weaken or deny constitutional
protection finding such firearms to be “unusually
dangerous,” akin to Bowie Knives. Id. at 244–50.
Under Miller and the 19 th century state cases
discussed above, those “military” features point
toward the militia function, and constitutional
protection.
Grant, like Bevis, also wrongly limits arms
protection exclusively to personal self-defense, and is
thus inconsistent with Heller’s acknowledgment of the
other lawful purposes for which the Second
Amendment was enacted, such as hunting, target
shooting and most importantly here, preserving a well
trained populace capable of effectively serving in the
militia. Heller, 554 U.S. at 599.
Heller described self-defense  as “the central
component” of the right, 554 U.S. at 599, but never
said it was the only lawful purpose for arms possession.
The opinion specifically identified preservation of the
citizen militia as the pu rpose announced by the
preface. Id. at 598–99. A central component is not an
exclusive component, and an ordinary rifle does not
lose protection because ju dges consider a handgun a
more appropriate arm for  a particular defensive
scenario.
Grant nevertheless contrasted AR-15s with handguns, reasoning that rifles may be longer, heavier,

21


harder for an inexperienced user to maneuver indoors,
and more capable of penetration. 153 F.4th at 241.
Aside from ignoring AR-15s utility for common
defense, Heller forecloses substitute-weapon reasoning.
The District could not ban handguns because long
guns remained available; citizens were entitled to
choose commonly possessed arms for self defense. See
554 U.S. at 629. The constitutional vice is not cured
by leaving “more than 1,000” government-approved
firearms on the market. Nat’l Ass’n for Gun Rights ,
153 F.4th at 242. The First Amendment would not
tolerate a ban on one protected medium because a
thousand others remain.
Nor may heightened lethality resolve the case.
Every firearm is dangerous. Caetano held that
dangerousness alone is insufficient; the historical rule
concerns weapons that are both dangerous and
unusual. See 577 U.S. at 417 (Alito, J., concurring). An
arm commonly possessed by law-abiding citizens
cannot simultaneously be “unusual” in the constitutionally relevant sense. See Heller, 554 U.S. at 627.
Heller made this crystal clear when it explained that
“unusual” means “highly unusual in society at
large.” Id. The government may punish misuse and
disarm persons shown to threaten others under
historically grounded principles. See United States v.
Rahimi, 602 U.S. 680, 693–700 (2024). It may not
prohibit possession of common arms by relabeling
their effectiveness as unusually dangerous.
Finally, the Second Circuit’s invocation of Bowie
knives, percussion pistols, and laws regulating
concealed carry does not establish a tradition of

22


banning possession of common rifles. See Nat’l Ass’n
for Gun Rights, 153 F.4th at 236, 242-445; Id. at 251–
52 (Nathan, J., concurring). Bruen requires relevant
similarity in “how and why” historical and modern
regulations burden the right. See 597 U.S. at 29–31.
And that test is not met here. First, Bowie knives and
many pistols were not consid ered to have utility for
the militia. See, e.g., Fife v. State, 31 Ark. at 460–61.
Second, regulations of manne r, misuse, or concealed
carry are not analogues to a flat ban on keeping an
entire class of arms in the home. See Heller, 554 U.S.
at 629. Cf. Bruen, 597 U.S. at 52-54 (concealed carry
prohibitions did not justify outright bans on carry).
The supposed historical analogues fail at a more
basic level. Bowie-knife statutes often regulated
concealed carry or enhanced  punishment for misuse;
they did not generally prohibit peaceable citizens from
keeping the knives in the home. Hanson v. District of
Columbia, 120 F.4th 223, 272-73 (D.C. Cir. 2024)
(Walker, J., dissenting). Trap-gun and discharge laws
regulated dangerous conduct. Gunpowder-storage
laws regulated how volatile material was kept in dense
places. None rested on the principle that an ordinary
arm could be prohibited because criminals might
inflict greater harm with it. The relevant “why” was
manner-specific danger, not suppression of civilian
militia capability; the relevant “how” was regulation,
not categorical disarmament.
Grant also revives interest balancing under
historical labels. Its disc ussion of wall penetration,
mass shootings, rates of fire, and alternative firearms
asks whether Connecticut made a reasonable policy

23


choice. See 153 F.4th at 247. Bruen rejected that
inquiry because the Second Amendment already
embodies the constitutional balance. 597 U.S. at 25–
26 & n.6. Modern empirical claims may inform
legislation within constitutional bounds, but they
cannot substitute for a historical tradition of
comparable restriction.
C. Bianchi illustrates the same inversion.
Although Bianchi is not under review, its en banc
reasoning demonstrates entrenched error that has
infected lower courts. The Fourth Circuit reaffirmed
its view that Heller said that arms “‘like’ M-16
rifles”—those “most useful in military service”—fall
outside the Amendment, and asserted Bruen left that
categorical holding intact. Bianchi v. Brown , 111
F.4th 438, 451–52 (4th Cir. 2024) (en banc).
Heller’s discussion of M-16s cannot bear that
weight. Heller stated the right was not limited to arms
useful in warfare and cautioned that “M-16 rifles and
the like” may be banned. 554 U.S. at 624–28. But it
derived the protected category from Miller: weapons
commonly possessed by law-abiding citizens and thus
brought to militia duty. Id. at 624–25, 627. Whatever
the precise boundary for machineguns, which are not
commonly possessed, Heller did not announce that
semiautomatic rifles become unprotected when
military forces value accu rate semiautomatic fire.
Staples confirms the legal and functional distinction:
an AR-15 ordinarily fires only one shot per trigger
press, unlike an automatic M-16. See 511 U.S. at 602
& n.1.

24


Bianchi’s rule would produce the constitutional
absurdity identified by Baude and Leider: legislatures
may ban a rifle because its features make it useful for
the very militia which the Second Amendment sought
to preserve. 99 Notre Dame L. Rev. at 1501–02. This
Court should reject that inversion expressly, lest the
operative clause remain individual in name but
stripped of the arms needed to fulfill the announced
purpose of the preamble.
The phrase “M-16 rifles and the like” is dicta
addressing the outer boundary of protection, not a
license to ban any weapon sharing ergonomic features
or ammunition with a service rifle. See Heller,  554
U.S. at 627. Read in context, the sentence follows
Heller’s explanation that modern limits may constrain
militia effectiveness but do not alter the historical
meaning of the right. Id. at 627–28. Heller did not
silently overrule Miller’s holding that militia
relationship supports prot ection. At minimum, “and
the like” must preserve the distinction between
machineguns and ordinary commonly possessed
semiautomatic rifles that this Court recognized in
Staples, 511 U.S. at 602 & n.1.
Bianchi’s reliance on rifle features it terms
military that promote  accuracy, controllability, and
capacity is particularly incompatible with common
defense. Those qualities help a citizen hit an intended
target, provide for rapid follow-up shots if needed, and
avoid unintended harm. A pistol grip improves
control; an adjustable stock permits fit to body size; a
flash suppressor can preserve the shooter’s vision in
low light; detachable magazines permit reliable

25


reloading. That soldiers value function does not make
function constitutionally suspect. The founding militia
laws demanded effective ar ms in working order, not
deliberately inferior substitutes. See Miller, 307 U.S.
at 179–82.
III. AR-15 Type Rifles Are “Arms,” Are Commonly
Possessed, And Cannot Be Banned.
The Court can resolve these cases without
inventing a new test. First, AR-15 platform and
similar semiautomatic rifles are plainly bearable
arms. Heller, 554 U.S. at 582. Caetano makes clear
that the category was not frozen in 1791 and extends
prima facie to modern instruments. 577 U.S. at 411–
12 (per curiam).
Second, these rifles are commonly possessed by
law-abiding citizens for lawful purposes. The petitions
document millions of rifles in civilian hands and
describe the AR-15 as the Nation’s most popular rifle.
Pet. Viramontes v. Cook County , No. 25-238 at 5–10
(Aug. 27, 2025); Pet. Grant v. Higgins, No. 25-566 at
5–13, (Nov. 7, 2025). Common possession defeats the
“unusual” half of “dangerous and unusual.” Heller,
554 U.S. at 627. See Caetano , 577 U.S. at 417–18
(Alito, J., concurring).
Third, respondents cannot identify a historical
tradition of banning possession of ordinary militiasuitable rifles by peaceable citizens. Founding-era law
generally required such citizens to acquire and
maintain arms suitable for the militia. See Miller, 307
U.S. at 179–82; Act of May 8, 1792, ch. 33, § 1, 1 Stat.
271.

26


Respondents may invoke concerns for public safety
such as mass shootings. Those incidents, while rare
compared to criminal mi suse of handguns, are
certainly grave, but Bruen forecloses judicial interest
balancing. 597 U.S. at 22–23. The Constitution itself
reflects a judgment that an armed citizenry contributes
to the security of a free State, notwithstanding risks
that attend to the people possessing weapons. Courts
must apply that judgment through text and history,
not replace it with their assessments of which arms
citizens need.
A clear rule follows: a State may not ban
possession of a bearable rifle that is commonly kept by
law-abiding citizens for lawf ul purposes. The rifle’s
usefulness for militia service strengthens rather than
defeats the textual and historical case. That rule
respects Heller’s individual right, Miller’s militiacentered arms inquiry, Caetano’s treatment of modern
weapons, and Bruen’s allocation of the historical
burden.
A. “Common use” reflects civilian possession
before the call to service.
The common-use principle is sometimes treated as
a bare numerical test. Numbers matter because
widespread lawful possession forecloses the label
“unusual.” But the principl e has deeper historical
logic. Miller and Heller refer to citizens appearing for
service with arms supplied by themselves. Miller, 307
U.S. at 179; Heller, 554 U.S. at 624–25. Common
civilian possession is therefore not an accidental proxy
for constitutional status. It is the mechanism through
which a citizen militia remains possible.

27


That mechanism also defeats circularity. A
government cannot manufacture unusualness by
banning a protected arm early and then rely on the
ban’s success to prove that the arm is uncommon.
Caetano rejected temporal freezing, 577 U.S. at 411–12,
and Bruen rejected using twentieth-century restrictions
to contradict the founding understanding of the right.
See 597 U.S. at 66 & n. 28.
B. The common-defense theory identifies a
floor, not an exclusive limit.
Recognizing common defen se does not require
retreat from Heller’s protection of personal selfdefense. A right may serve multiple lawful purposes.
The same rifle may protect a household during a
violent emergency, defen d a community when civil
order collapses, and furnish useful familiarity if its
owner is called for public service. Heller’s point was
that actual militia enrollm ent does not condition the
individual right which belongs to the people in
general. See 554 U.S. at 581, 592.
The Court therefore need not decide every question
which may arise from the common-defense theory.
This case concerns rifles that are bearable, commonly
possessed, and suitable for the traditional functions of
an individually equipped citizen. On the historical
evidence, those rifles lie at the protected core under
both Heller’s self-defense reasoning and the
Amendment’s common-defense purpose. Accordingly,
the Second Amendment protects their possession and
mandates reversal of the decisions below.

28


CONCLUSION
The judgments of the courts of appeals should be
reversed.
